procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but implied to be a lower criminal court in Uttar Pradesh, India, as the High Court appeals were against convictions.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 21st September, 1973 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1923 & 1918 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Nine accused persons, including Om Prakash (A-1) and Anoop Singh (A-2), were convicted by a lower court. They appealed their convictions to the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 1918 and 1923 of 1969. The Allahabad High Court dismissed these appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused persons (appellants) approached the Supreme Court by Special Leave, challenging the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of their appeals. The Supreme Court case numbers are Criminal Appeals Nos. 54 & 55 of 1974.

arguments.issue_text: The credibility and reliability of the evidence given by witness P.W. 2.
appellant_arguments: P.W. 2 has modulated her evidence to fit in with the prosecution's case and therefore should not be relied upon for a conviction.
respondent_arguments: P.W. 2 gave straightforward evidence without any attempt at making improvements to fit the testimony of other witnesses, and her evidence is wholly reliable.

arguments.issue_text: The significance of lower courts disbelieving or not relying on other prosecution witnesses (P.Ws 1, 7, and 8).
appellant_arguments: The fact that the Sessions Judge disbelieved P.Ws 1 and 7, and the High Court did not rely on P.W. 8, weakens the prosecution's case.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts erred in rejecting the evidence of P.Ws 1, 7, and 8. Their evidence should be considered to the extent that it is corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 2, as it lends assurance to her testimony about the appellants' presence at the scene.

arguments.issue_text: The lack of recovery of any looted property from the appellants.
appellant_arguments: Since no property looted from the house was recovered from any of the appellants, it is improbable that they were responsible for the crime.
respondent_arguments: The lack of recovery is not fatal to the prosecution's case, given the availability of other incriminating evidence against the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: The alternative theory that an unknown gang committed the crime.
appellant_arguments: An unknown armed gang of dacoits committed the crime, and the accused have been falsely implicated due to enmity.
respondent_arguments: There is sufficient incriminating evidence against the appellants to prove their involvement, making the 'unknown gang' theory untenable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the First Information Report (FIR) was ante-timed.
appellant_arguments: The First Information Report (Exh. Ka-1) is ante-timed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mere non-recovery of looted property from an accused is not, by itself, a sufficient basis to conclude that the accused is not the culprit, especially when other incriminating evidence exists.
obiter: The evidence of a witness who gives straightforward testimony without any attempt at making improvements to fit in with other prosecution witnesses can be considered wholly reliable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution has proven its case against the appellants beyond a reasonable doubt. The conviction is upheld based on the evidence of P.W. 2, which is considered reliable and is lent assurance by the testimony of other witnesses (P.Ws 1, 7, and 8) regarding the presence of the appellants at the scene. The lack of recovery of looted property is not fatal to the prosecution's case in light of the other sufficient incriminating evidence.
legal_tests_applied: The standard of proof in a criminal case is 'beyond all reasonable doubt'.

The evidence of witnesses partially disbelieved by lower courts can still be used to the extent that it is corroborated by a reliable primary witness, as it lends assurance to that witness's testimony.
The non-recovery of looted property is not fatal to a conviction for dacoity if there is other sufficient incriminating evidence to prove the crime.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the disbelief of other witnesses (P.Ws 1, 7, 8) by lower courts weakened the case. Instead, the Supreme Court held that the lower courts erred in rejecting their evidence entirely, as it served to corroborate P.W. 2's testimony about the appellants' presence.

The court explicitly dismissed the argument that the non-recovery of looted property was exculpatory, stating: 'From the mere fact that none of the looted properties had been recovered from any of the appellants it could not be said that they were not the culprits in the case.'
The alternative theory of an unknown gang was rejected because the court found there was 'enough incriminating evidence against' the appellants.
why_respondent_won: The court found the evidence of P.W. 2 to be the reliable core of the prosecution's case.

The court held that the evidence of P.Ws 1, 7, and 8, far from weakening the case, actually 'lends assurance to the evidence of P.W. 2 that the appellants entered the house and assaulted her husband fatally and that some of them caused injuries to her and committed decoity.'
The court determined that the lack of recovery of property was not a fatal flaw in the prosecution's case because there was 'enough incriminating evidence against them' to secure a conviction.
